sections.h2: Is a cash offer or a listing better for a house in Durham, NC?
sections.html:
A listing usually targets the highest price, and a cash offer targets speed and fewer moving parts. Durham sellers who need a quick closing, a repair-free sale or a clean exit from an inherited or rented house often look at both.

Durham is a renter-heavy city, which affects who is likely to buy. The Census Bureau puts the owner-occupied housing unit rate at 52.3 percent for 2020 to 2024, well under the shares in most North Carolina suburbs. Investors and landlords are part of the buyer pool alongside owner-occupants.

  • List when the house shows well and you can wait through inspections and the buyer's loan approval.
  • Sell by owner if you can price the house and run the contract yourself.
  • Take a cash offer when repairs, tenants, probate or a deadline make a normal listing hard.

The deed is recorded with the Durham County Register of Deeds. State law ranks competing conveyances by the time of registration in the county where the land sits.

sections.h2: What does Durham look like for a house seller?
sections.html:
Durham is the largest city in Durham County, with 305,561 residents in the Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate and 112.79 square miles of land. The 2020 Census count was 283,506, up from 228,330 in 2010.

The city's economy leans on health care and education. QuickFacts lists 2022 health care and social assistance receipts at 6,106,797 thousand dollars, more than four times the city's accommodation and food services sales of 1,277,689 thousand dollars. Some 57.3 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher, and the mean commute is 22.3 minutes.

sections.h2: When does Durham County revalue property, and what is the next date?
sections.html:
Durham County's most recent revaluation took effect January 1, 2025, and the county says the next reappraisal is January 1, 2029. State law requires every county to reappraise at least every eight years, and a county can advance the date by resolution.

The county explains that an eight-year gap in a fast-growing county invites larger and less predictable jumps, which is why it shortened the cycle. Between revaluations, a value can still change for new construction, a change in zoning, or a parcel split, and the county then applies the rates built for the last reappraisal year. A house built in 2026 on a lot that was vacant in 2025, the county's own example, is appraised at January 1, 2025 market values.

  • The tax office values at 100 percent of fair market value as of the effective date.
  • Appraisal and taxation are separate: each taxing body sets its own rate.
  • Measurements are taken from outside, so square footage can differ from a fee appraisal.

If the buyer asks about taxes on a newly built house, the county suggests having the closing attorney estimate the bill from the sale price. That figure is an estimate only.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Durham County property value?
sections.html:
File through the county's Tax Help portal, which the county recommends, or on a paper form, and do it before the Board of Equalization and Review adjourns. You can also file within 30 days of a change of value notice. The county's call center number is 919-560-0300.

The adjournment date is published in the Durham Herald-Sun and on the county website. For 2025 it was June 16, 2025 at 5:00 p.m., a date that has passed, so use the notice you receive for the current year. Appeal reviews can take 30 to 120 days, and the county says affordability and the size of a bill change are not grounds.

  • Support your appeal with comparable sales. For the 2025 cycle the county looked at 2023 and 2024 market sales and excluded related-party sales, foreclosures, short sales and auctions.
  • A fee appraisal or settlement statement near January 1, 2025 may help. One sale alone may not reflect the typical price.
  • A lowered value is not retroactive: G.S. 105-287 makes it effective for the year it is made.

The Board of Equalization and Review has five citizens, each appointed by one county commissioner. Owners may attend a hearing, though the board decides on the documents if you cannot. After the board, you have 30 days from the mailed decision to go to the state Property Tax Commission.

sections.h2: Who can file the appeal when an heir or an LLC owns the house?
sections.html:
For a house owned by an individual, the owner, a North Carolina licensed attorney or someone holding a power of attorney can file, but only the owner or an attorney can speak for the owner at the hearing. Durham treats the board as quasi-judicial, so representation there can be the practice of law.

For a business entity, the list is narrower: an attorney, an officer, a manager or member-manager of an LLC, a W-2 employee the entity authorizes, or an owner with at least 25 percent. All but the attorney must file a Non-Attorney Representative Authorization. A power of attorney cannot file for a business entity.

If you are handling an inherited house, confirm who holds title as of January 1, because the county says ownership is determined annually as of that date. Forward any notice that reaches you after a sale to the new owner.

sections.h2: What tax relief and present-use programs exist for Durham owners?
sections.html:
North Carolina has three relief programs, and each owner can use only one. They are the elderly or disabled exclusion, the disabled veteran exclusion and the circuit breaker, and the county assessor accepts the applications.

  • Elderly or disabled: the greater of $25,000 or 50 percent of appraised value, with a 2026 income limit that NCDOR prints as $38,800.
  • Disabled veteran: the first $45,000 of appraised value, with no age or income limit on the form.
  • Circuit breaker: 4 percent of income up to the limit, 5 percent above it up to 150 percent of the limit, with the excess deferred as a lien.

Durham's Real Property FAQ separately describes the present-use program, which covers agriculture (a tract of at least 10 acres in production with an average gross income of at least $1,000 for three years), horticulture (at least 5 acres) and forestry (at least 20 acres). Veterans in Durham number 11,287 by the Census count for 2020 to 2024, so the veteran exclusion is worth checking.

sections.h2: What are the closing costs and recording rules when selling in Durham?
sections.html:
The seller pays the excise tax on the deed before recording at the Register of Deeds, set at $1.00 for each $500, or fractional part, of the price. The county keeps half and the state receives the rest.

Recording fees are uniform statewide. An ordinary instrument costs $26.00 for the first 15 pages and $4.00 per extra page, and a deed of trust costs $64.00 for the first 35 pages. A certified copy costs $5.00 for the first page and $2.00 for each additional one.

The year's property tax is a lien dating from the January listing date. Ask the closing attorney to check that Durham County shows the bill paid or arranged before funds move.

sections.h2: What Durham zoning and landlord rules matter before I sell?
sections.html:
Durham's Unified Development Ordinance allows only one accessory dwelling on a lot. Its heated floor area is capped at 1,000 square feet for a single-story unit and 1,200 square feet total, with a different cap in the rural district. A buyer planning a backyard unit should ask the city planning staff to confirm the rules for the specific lot.

  • Tenants: a month-to-month tenancy ends on 7 days' notice, and nonpayment can lead to forfeiture 10 days after demand.
  • Foreclosure: the clerk of superior court holds the hearing, notice is due at least 10 days before it, and an upset bid must exceed the last bid by at least 5 percent with a $750 minimum.
  • Probate: an affidavit can settle an intestate estate of $20,000 or less after 30 days. North Carolina repealed its estate tax for deaths on or after January 1, 2013.

Tell a buyer about any lease and any permit work done on the house.

faqs.q: Who values and taxes a house in Durham?
faqs.a: Durham County values it and bills it. Each taxing body sets its own rate, and the final bill cannot be known until those rates are set.

faqs.q: When is the next Durham County reappraisal?
faqs.a: The county says January 1, 2029. The most recent one took effect January 1, 2025.

faqs.q: Can I get a refund for past years if my value is lowered?
faqs.a: No. G.S. 105-287 makes a change effective for the year it is made and not retroactive.

faqs.q: How long does a Durham appeal review take?
faqs.a: The county says anywhere from 30 to 120 days, depending on how many appeals come from your neighborhood.

faqs.q: Do I need to be home for a county appraiser visit?
faqs.a: Not unless the appraiser needs to see the inside. Measurements are taken from the outside, and an appointment is made first if access is needed.
